frontmatter.title: Fresh Cabbage, Cucumber and Radish Kimchi
ingredients: 3 lbs Napa Cabbage, halved and cut into 2-inch pieces

exactBefore.body:
## Chef's Note

This is fresh kimchi ready to eat immediately. The key to crisp, non-watery kimchi is salting the vegetables heavily for an hour to draw out excess moisture that would otherwise dilute the spice paste. Using three vegetables - cabbage, cucumber, and daikon - ensures a complex texture in every bite. Always use gochugaru; the specific smoky heat is essential to authentic kimchi.

## Directions

1.  **The Cure:** In four separate large bowls, divide the cabbage, cucumbers, daikon, and radishes. Sprinkle 2 tbsp of salt into each bowl and toss well. **Let stand for 1 hour** at room temperature.
2.  **The Paste:** In a high-powered blender, combine ginger, garlic, gochugaru, rice vinegar, sesame oil, fish sauce, scallions, and sugar. Puree until almost smooth.
3.  **The Rinse:** Drain the vegetables thoroughly. Gently squeeze each handful to remove all remaining water.
4.  **The Bind:** In one massive bowl, toss all the vegetables with the kimchi paste until every piece is uniformly coated in the deep red glaze.
5.  **The Finish:** Transfer to glass jars. Cover and refrigerate for **at least 4 hours** (ideally 24) to allow the flavors to meld and the fermentation to begin.
6.  **Serve:** This fresh kimchi (Geotjeori style) is at its best within the first week.

frontmatter.title: Fresh Cabbage, Cucumber and Radish Kimchi
frontmatter.totalTime: About 5½–6 hours, including salting and at least 4 hours chilling
ingredients: 3 lbs napa cabbage, cored and cut into 2-inch pieces
1 1/4 lbs daikon radish, peeled and cut into 1/2-inch pieces
67 g kosher salt, for salting the vegetables; weigh this amount for any brand
4 oz fresh ginger, peeled and coarsely chopped
1/4 cup plus 2 tbsp unseasoned rice vinegar

learning.focus: Salt and drain vegetables before coating them with a concentrated ginger-gochugaru dressing.
learning.outcome: Crisp, seasoned cabbage, cucumber and two kinds of radish with a clinging spicy dressing.
before: Wash and dry the produce before cutting it; use clean bowls and utensils kept separate from raw meat and seafood.
Use a scale for the displayed kosher-salt amount; the same weight works with any brand. Equal volumes of different salts can weigh differently.
The source makes about 12 cups. Vegetable size and how much liquid drains away change the actual yield, so have enough covered containers ready.

checkpoints.cue: Each vegetable has its own bowl and one-quarter of the listed salt.
checkpoints.why: The source gives the same salt allocation to four different vegetable loads. Weighing the total removes brand-density variation without inventing a uniform percentage cure.

checkpoints.cue: Each bowl has released liquid, and gently squeezed handfuls no longer shed a stream of it.
checkpoints.why: Draining and gentle squeezing keep the vegetable liquid from thinning the dressing. The source does not rinse away the cure.

checkpoints.cue: All the dressing is distributed over the vegetables.
checkpoints.why: The vinegar, oil, fish sauce, ginger and chile each belong to the finished dish; none is a reserved brine.

troubleshooting.problem: The dressing pools at the bottom.
troubleshooting.cause: The vegetables continued releasing moisture or were not drained thoroughly.
troubleshooting.fix: Toss before serving. On the next batch, drain each vegetable well and squeeze gently before adding the full dressing.

troubleshooting.problem: The batch tastes saltier than expected.
troubleshooting.cause: Vegetable sizes and retained cure vary, and fish sauce adds salt after draining.
troubleshooting.fix: Serve it in small side portions with unsalted rice or other plain food. Use the stated salt weight for the next batch rather than measuring a denser brand by the half cup.

substitutions.alternative: The source’s hot sesame oil, in the same listed amount
substitutions.effect: Hot sesame oil adds chile heat; toasted sesame oil gives a nuttier finish. Gochugaru remains in either version.

learning.storage: Keep covered at 40°F or colder and use within 3–4 days of preparation, including the first chilling period. This is a conservative fresh-food limit; the salting and vinegar do not establish a longer keeping time. Use clean utensils and return the container to the refrigerator promptly. Keep total room-temperature preparation and serving time under 2 hours, or under 1 hour above 90°F.
learning.timing: Allow 30–45 minutes of hands-on preparation, 1 hour salting and at least 4 hours chilling. Making the dressing during the salting period overlaps part of the active work, so plan about 5½–6 hours from the first chopping. Refrigerating the finished kimchi overnight fits the make-ahead schedule, but does not restart its storage clock. At another batch size, give each vegetable its own bowl, divide the displayed salt total into four equal portions and use enough mixing and refrigerator capacity; the rests do not multiply.

exactAfter.body:
## Chef's Note

Ginger, gochugaru and rice vinegar give this fresh kimchi its punch, while cabbage, cucumber, daikon and small radishes provide different textures. Salt them separately, then drain and gently squeeze before adding the dressing. The original batch makes about 12 cups, depending on vegetable size and draining, and needs at least four hours in the refrigerator before serving.

## Directions

1. **Salt the vegetables:** Put the cabbage, cucumbers, daikon and radishes in four separate large bowls. Divide the listed kosher salt into four equal portions and toss one portion thoroughly with each vegetable. Let stand for 1 hour, tossing once halfway through. Keep total room-temperature handling, including preparation, under 2 hours; if the kitchen is above 90°F, do this salting rest in the refrigerator.
2. **Blend the dressing:** While the vegetables rest, combine the ginger, garlic, gochugaru, unseasoned rice vinegar, toasted sesame oil, fish sauce, scallions and sugar in a blender. Purée until almost smooth. Keep the dressing refrigerated until the vegetables are ready.
3. **Drain and squeeze:** Drain each bowl thoroughly, discarding all the released liquid. Gently squeeze each handful to remove excess moisture without crushing the vegetables. Do not rinse after salting.
4. **Dress the vegetables:** In a very large bowl, toss all the drained vegetables with all the ginger-gochugaru dressing until evenly coated. If necessary, divide both vegetables and dressing between two bowls and combine the batches afterward.
5. **Chill:** Transfer to clean, shallow covered containers and refrigerate promptly at 40°F or colder for at least 4 hours before serving. An overnight chill gives the flavors more time to mingle.
6. **Serve cold:** Toss before serving, spoon out small side portions with a clean utensil and promptly return the remaining kimchi to the refrigerator. Use within 3–4 days of preparation.

saltDecision.selectionRationale: User authorized product recommendation. saltDecision.chemicalVsPacking: Both products are predominantly sodium chloride; a weighed generic-kosher dose avoids the large packing-density difference. Dissolution, vegetable water and salt discarded with drain liquid still vary.

saltDecision.retainedSalinity: Draining removes unknown amounts of water and dissolved salt. Squeezing removes more liquid. Fish sauce contributes additional retained salt after the cure. Final salinity cannot be computed from the initial salt mass, nominal12cups or a water-density assumption.

wholeRecipeReview.allocations: Every cabbage/cucumber/daikon/radish enters its own cure bowl and later the final mixture. All67g cure salt applied in four equal portions, some discarded with liquid. All eight dressing ingredients used completely; no reserve, reduction or invented diluent.
wholeRecipeReview.liquidAndDensity: Vinegar amount remains exact1/4cup+2tbsp=6tbsp, sesame oil3tbsp, fish sauce3tbsp. These do not establish pH, titratable acidity, salt concentration, water activity or microbial safety. No grams/liters conversion for drained vegetables or finished kimchi.
wholeRecipeReview.sourceDisagreements: Original sesame ingredient is hot sesame oil; current uses toasted sesame oil. Keep current3tbsp and preserve original same-quantity hot-oil option in learning; no silent restoration/deletion. Clarify unseasoned rice vinegar and large garlic/medium radish states from exact original.
wholeRecipeReview.process: All four vegetable bowls, one-hour salting, drain and gentle squeeze without rinse, full paste and minimum four-hour covered refrigeration retained. No step brings water into the recipe. Initial produce washing is FDA hygiene before curing.
wholeRecipeReview.capacity: Four separate bowls with space to toss all source vegetable loads; final very large bowl or two balanced mixing batches with all dressing allocated; clean shallow covered refrigerator containers. No guessed bowl-liter or jar count/tested fit.
wholeRecipeReview.heatAndTime: No cooking.30–45min active preparation with dressing overlapped during1h rest;4h minimum chill; about5.5–6h estimated elapsed. Overnight chill is optional meld time, not fermentation validation.
wholeRecipeReview.yield: Source nominal12cups remains about12cups. Counts, trim, vegetable size and drainage can change yield; no invented narrower range or demand for a kitchen measurement before editorial acceptance.
wholeRecipeReview.storage: Fresh refrigerated salad/kimchi route only.40°F maximum, conservative3–4days from preparation including first chill, clean utensils, promptly returned cold storage, cumulative2h/1h handling rule. No shelf-stability, canning, probiotic, controlled fermentation or one-week guarantee.
wholeRecipeReview.scaling: Amounts scale proportionally; one-quarter displayed salt total to each vegetable bowl at any size. Rest times and packing geometry do not multiply. Larger preparation loads must fit the same cumulative room-temperature limit; refrigerator holding and multiple bowls/containers apply.
